title: Big Data Concepts and Cloud Basics
summary: Most beginner projects fit comfortably in Pandas on a laptop, but real organizations often have data too large for one machine's memory, and understanding how that's handled is important context even at the beginner level. Big data is often described
content:
# Big Data Concepts and Cloud Basics ##### The Spark cluster that was slower than a laptop A team in Bengaluru moved their nightly analytics job to a five-node Spark cluster. The dataset was 8 GB. Runtime went from 4 minutes in Pandas to 11 minutes in Spark, and the cluster cost ₹32,000 a month. Distributed computing has real overhead — serialising data, shipping it across the network, coordinating executors, starting a JVM. Below a certain size that overhead dominates, and a single machine with enough RAM wins comfortably. Their 8 GB fitted in memory. The correct move was a bigger laptop, or switching to Polars. The genuine threshold for distribution is higher than most people assume — commonly somewhere past a few hundred gigabytes, or when the job must span multiple machines for reasons other than size. Knowing where that line sits, and recognising which side you are on, is worth more than knowing Spark's API. ##### The three Vs The classic framing of "big data" — and it is worth noting that two of the three have nothing to do with size. **Volume** — the data does not fit in one machine's memory or disk. This is what people mean by big data, and it is often the least interesting constraint. A machine with 256 GB of RAM is cheap to rent by the hour. **Velocity** — data arrives continuously and must be processed as it comes. A payments system handling 40,000 transactions per second cannot batch overnight. This is frequently the *real* driver of distributed architecture. **Variety** — structured tables, JSON logs, images, PDFs, audio, all needing to live together. Relational databases handle the first well and the rest badly. Later additions include **veracity** (data quality and trustworthiness) and **value** (whether any of it is worth processing). A practical size ladder for deciding where you actually are: | Data size | Tool | Notes | |---|---|---| | Under ~1 GB | Pandas | No thought required | | 1–20 GB | Pandas with dtype optimisation, or Polars | Fixing dtypes often solves it entirely | | 20 GB – 1 TB | Polars streaming, DuckDB, or a big cloud VM | Single machine, still | | 1 TB+ | Spark, BigQuery, distributed systems | Now distribution earns its cost | | Continuous streams | Kafka + Flink/Spark Streaming | Velocity, not volume | **Escalate deliberately.** Most "we need Spark" conversations end when someone checks memory usage with `deep=True` and converts three object columns to `category`. ##### Distributed computing intuition The core idea is old and simple: split the work across machines, process the pieces in parallel, and combine the results. **MapReduce** (Dean & Ghemawat, 2004) formalised it as two phases. **Map** applies a function to each record independently, producing key-value pairs. **Shuffle** groups all pairs with the same key onto the same machine. **Reduce** aggregates each group. ```mermaid flowchart TD A[8 TB of logs] --> B1[Node 1: chunk] A --> B2[Node 2: chunk] A --> B3[Node 3: chunk] B1 --> M1["MAP: emit city, 1"] B2 --> M2["MAP: emit city, 1"] B3 --> M3["MAP: emit city, 1"] M1 --> S{{"SHUFFLE: group by key
across the network"}} M2 --> S M3 --> S S --> R1[REDUCE: sum for Pune] S --> R2[REDUCE: sum for Mumbai] R1 --> O[Result] R2 --> O ``` The **shuffle** is the expensive step and the thing to understand. Map and reduce are local and parallel; shuffle moves data across the network. Any operation requiring a shuffle — `groupBy`, `join`, `distinct`, sorting — is orders of magnitude more expensive than one that does not. Most Spark performance work is about minimising shuffles. **Spark** improved on MapReduce mainly by keeping intermediate results in memory rather than writing to disk between every stage, which made iterative work (like machine learning) dramatically faster. Two Spark concepts worth knowing: **Lazy evaluation.** Transformations (`filter`, `select`, `groupBy`) build a plan and execute nothing. Only an **action** (`show`, `count`, `collect`, `write`) triggers computation. This lets the optimiser rearrange your whole query before running it — pushing filters earlier, combining steps, choosing join strategies. **Partitions.** A Spark DataFrame is split into chunks distributed across executors. Partition count and size determine parallelism, and getting it wrong is the most common cause of poor performance. ##### PySpark basics ```python from pyspark.sql import SparkSession from pyspark.sql import functions as F spark = (SparkSession.builder .appName("sales-analysis") .config("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true") # runtime optimisation .config("spark.driver.memory", "4g") .getOrCreate()) df = spark.read.csv("data/sales.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True) # Better in production: declare the schema explicitly, inferSchema reads the file twice df = spark.read.parquet("data/sales.parquet") df.printSchema() print(df.count(), len(df.columns)) df.show(5, truncate=False) ``` The API deliberately resembles Pandas, with important differences: ```python # Selecting and filtering df.select("city", "amount_inr").show(5) df.filter(F.col("amount_inr") > 5000).show(5) df.filter((F.col("status") == "paid") & (F.col("city") == "Pune")).show(5) # New columns df = df.withColumn("amount_lakh", F.round(F.col("amount_inr") / 100_000, 2)) df = df.withColumn("is_large", F.when(F.col("amount_inr") > 50_000, 1).otherwise(0)) # Grouped aggregation summary = (df .filter(F.col("status") == "paid") .groupBy("city", "category") .agg( F.count("*").alias("orders"), F.sum("amount_inr").alias("revenue"), F.round(F.avg("amount_inr"), 2).alias("avg_order"), F.countDistinct("customer_id").alias("customers"), ) .orderBy(F.desc("revenue"))) summary.show(10) # ACTION — everything runs now summary.explain(True) # inspect the physical plan # Joins enriched = df.join(customers_df, on="customer_id", how="left") # Window functions work as in SQL from pyspark.sql.window import Window w = Window.partitionBy("city").orderBy(F.desc("amount_inr")) df = df.withColumn("rank_in_city", F.row_number().over(w)) # SQL directly df.createOrReplaceTempView("sales") spark.sql(""" SELECT city, SUM(amount_inr) AS revenue FROM sales WHERE status = 'paid' GROUP BY city ORDER BY revenue DESC """).show() # Writing out — partitioned for efficient later reads summary.write.mode("overwrite").partitionBy("city").parquet("output/summary") spark.stop() ``` | | Pandas | PySpark | |---|---|---| | Execution | Immediate | Lazy until an action | | Scale | One machine's RAM | Cluster | | Index | Yes | No | | Mutability | In place possible | Immutable — always returns new | | Row access | `df.iloc[5]` | Awkward; not designed for it | | Small-data speed | Faster | Slower (overhead) | The rule that catches everyone: **`collect()` brings all data to the driver machine and will crash it** on a large DataFrame. Use `show()`, `take(n)`, or `limit(n).toPandas()` instead. The common performance mistakes: too few partitions (no parallelism), too many tiny partitions (scheduler overhead — aim for 100–200 MB each), Python UDFs instead of built-in `F.` functions (10–100× slower because every row crosses the JVM-Python boundary), and forgetting `.cache()` when reusing a DataFrame multiple times. ##### Cloud platforms Cloud computing means renting infrastructure by the hour rather than buying servers. For data science the appeal is elasticity — spin up a 128 GB machine for four hours of model training, then shut it down. The three major providers offer near-equivalent services under different names: | Purpose | AWS | GCP | Azure | |---|---|---|---| | Object storage | S3 | Cloud Storage | Blob Storage | | Virtual machines | EC2 | Compute Engine | Virtual Machines | | Data warehouse | Redshift | **BigQuery** | Synapse | | Managed Spark | EMR | Dataproc | HDInsight | | Notebooks | SageMaker | Vertex AI Workbench | ML Studio | | Serverless functions | Lambda | Cloud Functions | Functions | | Managed databases | RDS | Cloud SQL | SQL Database | For a beginner, three things matter more than provider choice: **Object storage is the foundation.** S3 and its equivalents are cheap, effectively unlimited, and the default place raw data lives. Everything else reads from there. **BigQuery is worth knowing specifically.** It is serverless — you write SQL, it scales automatically, and you pay per byte scanned. That pricing model has one dangerous implication: `SELECT *` on a 40 TB table is a five-figure rupee mistake in one query. Always select specific columns and filter on the partition key. ```python from google.cloud import bigquery client = bigquery.Client() query = """ SELECT city, COUNT(*) AS orders, SUM(amount_inr) AS revenue FROM `project.dataset.sales` WHERE order_date >= '2026-01-01' -- partition filter: reduces bytes scanned GROUP BY city ORDER BY revenue DESC """ job_config = bigquery.QueryJobConfig(dry_run=True) dry = client.query(query, job_config=job_config) print(f"will scan {dry.total_bytes_processed / 1e9:.2f} GB") # CHECK before running df = client.query(query).to_dataframe() ``` That dry run is a habit worth forming — it tells you the cost before you incur it. **Cost discipline matters.** The recurring cloud horror story is a GPU instance left running over a weekend. Set billing alerts on day one, shut down what you are not using, and prefer managed serverless services over always-on VMs where you can. For learning, the free tiers are genuinely usable: Google Colab gives free GPU access, BigQuery includes 1 TB of free queries monthly, and AWS and GCP both offer trial credits. ##### Warehouses, lakes and lakehouses Three storage architectures with different jobs. **Data warehouse** — structured, cleaned, schema-on-write. You define the schema before loading, so everything conforms. Optimised for fast SQL analytics on known questions. Redshift, BigQuery, Snowflake. **Data lake** — raw files of any format, schema-on-read. Store everything cheaply now, figure out the structure when you query. S3 or GCS holding Parquet, JSON, images, logs. Flexible, and prone to becoming a "data swamp" where nobody knows what is in it or whether it is trustworthy. **Lakehouse** — the modern synthesis. Lake-style cheap object storage plus warehouse-style guarantees: ACID transactions, schema enforcement, and time travel. Delta Lake, Apache Iceberg, Apache Hudi. | | Warehouse | Lake | Lakehouse | |---|---|---|---| | Data | Structured only | Anything | Anything | | Schema | On write | On read | On write, evolvable | | Cost per TB | High | Very low | Low | | Query speed | Fast | Slower | Fast | | Transactions | Yes | No | Yes | | Best for | BI, dashboards | ML, raw archival | Both | The organising pattern most teams converge on is **medallion architecture**: bronze holds raw immutable data as it arrived, silver holds cleaned and validated tables, gold holds aggregated business-ready tables. Each layer is reproducible from the one above, which means a bug in cleaning is fixable without re-collecting anything. ##### Common mistakes - Reaching for Spark on data that fits comfortably in RAM. - Not checking `memory_usage(deep=True)` before declaring a size problem. - `collect()` on a large Spark DataFrame, crashing the driver. - Python UDFs in a hot path instead of built-in `F.` functions. - Partitions of 5 MB (overhead) or 8 GB (out of memory). - `SELECT *` in BigQuery, billed per byte scanned. - No billing alerts, discovering the cost at month end. - Cloud VMs left running when idle. - A data lake with no catalogue, becoming a swamp nobody trusts. - Learning Spark's API before understanding when distribution is warranted. ##### Hands-on Install PySpark locally and load a dataset into a Spark DataFrame. Perform filtering, `groupBy` and aggregation, and call `.explain(True)` to see the physical plan. Then do the identical analysis in Pandas and time both — on a small dataset Pandas will win, and understanding *why* (JVM startup, serialisation, no parallelism benefit at that scale) is the point of the exercise. Deliberately call `.collect()` on something reasonably large and observe the memory behaviour. For the mini-project, build a PySpark analysis on a moderately large dataset — a few gigabytes if you can find one, or generate synthetic data. Read from Parquet, perform grouped aggregations and at least one join, use a window function, and write partitioned Parquet output. Then write up the comparison honestly: where Spark helped, where it added friction, what the overhead cost, and at what dataset size you would actually recommend it for this workload. That judgement is the deliverable. For the assignment, write a one-page summary explaining when you would move from Pandas to Spark and what distinguishes a data warehouse from a data lake. Ground it in specifics — give the approximate size threshold, name the intermediate options (Polars, DuckDB, a bigger VM) you would try first, and describe a concrete scenario where each storage architecture is the right choice. ##### Key takeaways - Volume is only one of the three Vs; velocity and variety often drive architecture more than size does. - Distribution has real overhead — try dtype optimisation, Polars, DuckDB and a bigger machine before a cluster. - Spark is lazy and partition-based; the shuffle is expensive, so minimising `groupBy` and `join` operations is most of tuning. - Object storage is the foundation of cloud data work, and BigQuery's per-byte pricing makes `SELECT *` genuinely dangerous. - Warehouses enforce schema on write, lakes defer it, and lakehouses add transactions and time travel to cheap storage.
